title: Sutton's predictions v Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
Arsenal and Chelsea have both made 100% winning starts to the new season - but something has to give when they meet at Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

"I suspect Chelsea will give Arsenal lots of the ball and try to counter-attack quickly," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"The Blues have got some brilliant creativity in Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro, but the fact they are vulnerable at the back could undermine them."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week three, he takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, who is a Leicester City fan.

Kasabian's ninth album, Act III, is out on Friday, 4 September, and they tour the UK in December.

Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

It has been an eventful decade for Foxes fans since they won the Premier League title in 2016 - and not always an enjoyable one.

Since then, they have seen their side reach the Champions League quarter-finals, lift the FA Cup and Community Shield, win promotion from the Championship and suffer three relegations, including last season when they went down to League One.

"Promotion!" said Serge. "It has to be. I love the play-offs, so a win at Wembley would do me."

A new-look Leicester side took their first step towards bouncing back when they picked up their opening win of the season against Plymouth on Tuesday, but Serge added Russell Martin's youthful side will need time to fully find their feet in the third tier.

"I hope they get it," he said. "Patience is so important in football, and young teams should play with no fear."

Chris Sutton and Serge Pizzorno were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

My daughter's old maths teacher, Mr Fields, is an Ipswich fan and he is very excited about how ambitious the club has been since getting promoted. I think all their supporters must be the same.

Ipswich have spent almost £200m on a stack of new signings to try to stay in the Premier League and, watching them, it is clear they are not just planning to park the bus.

They will be confident for this game after beating Sunderland at home on the opening weekend and I am expecting them to have a real go at Liverpool too.

It will be interesting to see if new signing Bradley Barcola starts for the Reds, who seem to have a lot of attacking players who like to play off the left.

Boss Andoni Iraola has plenty of attacking options, but I still have concerns about them defensively, while his players adjust to his front-foot pressing style.

I am sure he will get it right eventually, but at the moment they are leaking goals and creaking at the back.

My gut feeling is Ipswich will score, but Liverpool will still edge the win after two successive 2-2 draws. If their attack clicks, it will be hard to keep them out.

Newcastle have started the season superbly with four points, and it feels like they have changed the mood at St James' Park after a difficult summer.

There's no doom and gloom about the place despite them losing several key players and, after predicting they would lose their first two games, I feel differently about their prospects now.

Things can change very quickly of course and a home defeat by Bournemouth would see a lot of that optimism disappear. But, so far, I've been really impressed by Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa looks like he has got his confidence back.

I like the way new manager Matthias Jaissle has set them up to hit teams on the counter-attack, and Nico Gonzalez looks like a sensible signing too.

I called Newcastle 'a development club' before their first game, because of the type of players they have bought and sold this summer, but while their midfield is quite youthful, they have now got Nico in there to give them a bit of extra clout.

This is still a tricky game to call, however.

Bournemouth haven't won yet, but only because they have let leads slip away late on, first against Manchester City and then at home to Everton.

Cherries boss Marco Rose is another manager who likes to play on the front foot and they are certainly capable of getting something here, even though I have gone for a home win.

I was spot on with my predictions for both of these teams last week, but I still don't feel very confident about calling the outcome of this game.

Brentford are a brilliant counter-attacking side who seem especially strong at home.

I was erring towards backing the Bees to win, like they did in this fixture last season, but then had second thoughts.

I backed the Black Cats to win their first two matches (see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page) because they are a well-organised team, with plenty of physicality and also a threat up top.

My concern for them is what happens when European football starts, but that hasn't happened yet. I don't see them losing this.

I am not really sure what to make of Brighton yet. They smashed Aston Villa on the opening weekend but then lost to Chelsea despite dominating possession in what was a really strange game.

Leeds can be quite cagey on the road under Daniel Farke, but they are very good at what they do, and they will be a threat on the break.

I am still going with Brighton to win because they are playing with freedom at the moment, but I don't see them keeping a clean sheet and this is going to be close.

Neither of these teams have got a point so far, as I predicted.

On top of his side's poor start to the season, one of the problems for Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage will be dealing with Ismaila Sarr after he did not get a move to Liverpool before the transfer window shut.

My worry for Fulham is they have become a Real Madrid feeder team, and their boss Alvaro Arbeloa has already got issues with his squad.

He stuck the boot into his players after their defeat by Sunderland, questioning their mentality.

A first win would be massive for both new managers, but I don't think either of them will get it here.

This is a tale of two Citys - one of whom has made the best of starts to the season, while the other has had the worst.

Manchester City wiped the floor with Crystal Palace last week but it was their comeback to beat Bournemouth at the Etihad which felt bigger, because it was the beginning of a new era under Enzo Maresca.

In contrast, Coventry City have had a terrible time. Not their 3-0 opening defeat at Arsenal, because they can forget about that, but they must feel so deflated after losing 1-0 at home to another promoted side in Hull last time out.

This game is more like the Arsenal one, in that no-one is expecting Coventry to get anything, but the upshot is they are likely to be left without a point or even a goal after their first three games.

There were some doubts about Manchester City after the way they lost the Community Shield against Arsenal, but they look a different proposition already.

Maresca has made more signings in the past few days, including Enzo Fernandez from his old club Chelsea for £125m. I've heard people question whether Fernandez is worth the big money that City paid, but Maresca knows him well and I see him as a great addition to their midfield.

I said before the Bournemouth game I didn't think they could win the title without Rodri, but they have rebuilt their midfield now with Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi joining Elliot Anderson as new signings, and they have got real strength in there now.

I like Erling Haaland's new haircut too. It suits him far more than a ponytail. He looks a bit rougher and tougher and I don't think Coventry will keep him out.

Nottingham Forest are waiting for their first win under Oliver Glasner but I felt they were unlucky to lose against Leeds and also to only draw at Liverpool.

I have been very disappointed with Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham so far, however, and not just because of their poor results.

When he came in at Brighton, De Zerbi built an amazing team in a short space of time and they were great to watch even if they made a few mistakes along the way.

In contrast, we still don't know what his Spurs team are about, even though they have spent an absolute fortune on players.

I think that's on De Zerbi because, although new players take time to gel, his side have put in two really insipid performances so far.

He has put that down to the team not being fully fit and blamed their pre-season schedule, but they should still be doing much better than they are - with no points and no goals so far.

Other clubs, with new managers as well as lots of new players, look much more organised so it is not an excuse.

Still, Spurs have surely got to improve soon, which is why I have got them down to pick up a first point here.

Hull will be on such a high after winning their first two games, and that makes this game even harder to predict.

The Tigers are really well organised and are not bothered about how much possession they have, they are just bothered about being effective when they do get the ball.

They defend the box brilliantly but there will still be a few weeks this season where teams run all over them because of the way they are set up.

Aston Villa won't necessarily do that, but I still think they will come out on top despite their poor start to the new campaign.

Ollie Watkins is a big loss but they have got Nicolas Jackson in to lead their line, who I think is a good signing.

It took Villa six games to register their first league win last season, but they won't have to wait as long this time.

Everton ended up keeping hold of young midfielder Harrison Armstrong but they made a mess of their attempts to sign another striker before the transfer window closed.

I know Thierno Barry comes in for criticism and his finishing is erratic, but at least they still have him to lead their line.

He scores some brilliant goals too, as does Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, so I don't think it will be all doom and gloom for Everton fans this season, despite their frustration at the moment.

As for Manchester United, well I know some of their supporters think I am down on them all the time.

So, I'd like to point out I backed them to win their first two games of the season and they are joint top of the table (below) based on my predictions.

This time, I'm going for a draw, but that would still be a decent result for Michael Carrick's side.

Arsenal were a bit clunky last time out against Aston Villa, while I love what Xabi Alonso is doing at Chelsea.

He doesn't care about possession, and that's not how Chelsea try to get results.

It's strange because I had a look at how his Bayer Leverkusen side lined up when they won the Bundesliga, and they were pretty dominant possession-wise.

So, it is quite alarming when you look at the two league games Chelsea have played and see how much of the ball they haven't had. Against Fulham they only had 38% possession and then against Brighton it was down to 25%.

I don't know whether that is by design or by just not having the players to dominate. They are still free-scoring, but they are conceding loads of goals too.

Whatever the reason, I don't see it changing here. Arsenal are so powerful and the only question mark around them is if they are a forward or two short.

Even so, you would not exactly say they have a real weakness anywhere. The beauty of Mikel Arteta's side is they can play in different ways.

They demolished Manchester City in the Community Shield with some pure football, and played some nice stuff against Coventry too, but then they were able to grind out a win at Aston Villa as well.

Ultimately, whether they are free-flowing or not, their organisation should see them through this game too.

Chris picked up his first win of the season after getting seven correct results - including three exact scores - from the 10 matches in week two.

After a slow start, five of his correct results - and two of his exact scores - came in the five games on Sunday and Monday.

That gave him a total of 160 points, enough to hold off a strong challenge from the BBC readers and AI.

The collective efforts of the readers helped them get six correct results, with two exact scores, for 120 points.

Like Chris, AI managed seven correct results, but with only one exact score, leaving it on 100 points.

Chris' guest, Royal Blood drummer Ben Thatcher, did not fare so well. He got four correct results with no exact scores, and ended up with 40 points.

"It's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it," Sutton said. "I am burying AI at the moment, which is a lovely feeling."

Everyone was right about three of the fixtures - Manchester City's win at Crystal Palace, Manchester United's victory over Ipswich and Arsenal's success at Aston Villa.

There were only two fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - Liverpool's draw with Nottingham Forest and Hull's win at Coventry.

From almost 37,000 predictions for the latter, only around 5,000 (15%) of you backed the Tigers to take the three points, and fewer than 1,500 (4%) went for them to win by a 1-0 scoreline.

fullText:
US tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan police

Sadiq Khan has agreed for his text messages and emails to be searched as part of a legal battle with Palantir, the high court has been told, after he prevented the US technology company from working with the Metropolitan police.

The London mayor stepped in to block a £50m deal between Palantir and the Met in May, with the artificial intelligence developer suing Khan’s office over the decision.

Legal representatives for the mayor said they “did not originally consider it necessary” for Khan to be among those to have their communications searched before next year’s court case. But they relented, citing persistence from Palantir.

Sarah Brown, Khan’s former director of communications, who now works for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will also have her correspondence searched.

The proposed two-year deal would have allowed Palantir, which works for the Israeli military and the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, to provide AI technology to automate intelligence analysis in criminal investigations.

But the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac), which oversees large Scotland Yard contracts, said there had been a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules. It said police had seriously considered only one supplier (Palantir).

After the announcement, Palantir accused Khan of “putting politics above public safety” before declaring in June that it planned to sue the London mayor.

At a preliminary hearing on Thursday, the high court was told Khan and more than a dozen other Mopac and Greater London Authority officials would be classed as “custodians”.

The designation means their digital communications, including text messages, WhatsApp messages, and Microsoft Teams chats – insofar as they exist – will be searched for anything relevant to the issues in the legal tussle. These will then be disclosed to Palantir.

Joseph Barrett KC, for the mayor’s office, said in written submissions: “Mopac did not originally consider it necessary or proportionate for the mayor to be added as a custodian, given that the decision was taken by the deputy mayor for policing and crime; his senior position; and the likelihood that any documents held by him would be held by other individuals.

“However, Palantir has persisted in its requests, and Mopac has consented on a pragmatic basis.”

Brown, who in July moved from the mayor’s office to be appointed director of communications at Downing Street, was also listed as a custodian, meaning she too will have her correspondence searched, the court heard.

The decision to include Brown comes after Palantir said in court documents outlining its claim that press articles regarding the mayor’s office vetoing the Met deal cited concerns about Palantir’s values and ethics. Mopac has confirmed Brown “initiated” press briefings about the move.

The date range for the communication searches is still to be determined.

 Mopac reportedly is demanding to see Palantir’s own internal documents related to the deal, which the company is said to be resisting.

fullText:
Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’

The president of OpenAI, Greg Brockman, has claimed the world has entered a new era of artificial general intelligence after the release of his company’s latest model, Astra, which it described as the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model”.

Brockman made the claim on Thursday as the San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern and a pause in Astra’s training.

Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI has defined it as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.

“I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.”

OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours.

Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.”

Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”.

Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training. They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts.

Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.

But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences.

On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol. On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources.

But OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said: “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.”

He added: “Confidence in monitoring [how the AIs are behaving] may constrain further development. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”

The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals.

The race to release ever-more advanced AIs comes as OpenAI pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). Anthropic is also targeting an IPO which could value it as high as $2tn.

Meanwhile, more than 1,000 employees at frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently signed a joint letter this summer that warned the companies were “under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration”. They called on the US government to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

title: Investor Gavin Baker says AI data centers are probably 'the best thing that has happened to working-class Americans'
description: Investor Gavin Baker said that AI data centers were "revitalizing all of these dying small towns all over America," but faced a messaging problem.
fullText:
Gavin Baker said AI companies could learn a thing or two from former Meta exec Sheryl Sandberg.

The Atreides Management investor said data centers are revitalizing "dying small towns" and the working class.

AI giants could share real-world examples of positive impacts, like Sandberg would do on Meta earnings calls, he said.

AI data centers have a branding problem, according to venture capitalist Gavin Baker.

Baker is a longtime tech investor. He serves as managing partner and chief investment officer at the hedge fund Atreides Management, which has invested in multiple data center-related companies, such as Crusoe. On "The A16z Show," he made the case for data centers, which have proven highly controversial in the US.

"It's probably the best thing that has ever happened to working-class Americans," Baker said. "It is revitalizing all of these dying small towns all over America."

Baker said that a college degree was becoming "significantly NPV negative" — or negative in net present value — because young people can become electricians, plumbers, and HVAC techs instead. Those blue-collar jobs make "ungodly amounts of money" amid the AI boom, he said.

An anti-college fever is sweeping through tech. One data center electrician told Business Insider that he skipped out on an undergraduate degree — and now earns $40 an hour.

Then there are the environmental concerns with data centers, from electricity usage to water consumption. Baker said that tech was "getting much better" at addressing these issues.

Data centers are "really, really, really good, and they're having a positive impact on the world," he said.

"We are re-industrializing America. And it's awesome," Baker said. "This is what everyone in both parties has wanted for a long time."

Baker has also advocated for data centers on X. He wrote on Saturday that "any politician opposed to data centers is unqualified to hold public office."

He clarified on Sunday that there were reasonable concerns about data centers about 18 months ago, but that "well-structured" projects addressed those concerns.

"This has been unambiguously awesome for blue-collar Americans," Baker said.

Baker pointed some of the blame at China. On the podcast, he said that there is an "organized, CCP-funded campaign" against data centers that gets "laundered through TikTok." Similar accusations have been leveled by Garry Tan and Kevin O'Leary.

The social media platform X said that it found a 200,000-strong Chinese bot farm, some of which were posting about data centers. A researcher told Business Insider that many of these bots had no followers or engagement.

title: I Tried Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google’s Latest AI Upgrade, and It (Mostly) Lives Up to the Hype
description: Gemini 3.8 Flash is faster and better at completing complex tasks, though for now you have to pay for it.
fullText:
Google has rolled out two new AI models: Gemini 3.8 Flash (the "intelligent workhorse model" for everyday prompting), and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber (available to "trusted defenders" for cybersecurity protection). While we only got Gemini 3.7 a matter of weeks ago, the new model brings with it some substantial improvements.

According to Google, reasoning and coding are better than ever with Gemini 3.8 Flash, and there are "significant" improvements across "software engineering, agentic tasks, and critical, multi-step reasoning in specialized domains"—so this is very much an update for advanced AI, rather than your basic prompting. You'll find Gemini 3.8 Flash available now inside the Gemini app if you use either the AI Pro plan ($19.99 a month) or the AI Ultra plan ($99.99 or $199.99 a month). There's nothing yet for users on the free tier or the $7.99-per-month AI Plus plan, though these models do trickle down to lower tiers over time, as upgrades are released.

You'd be forgiven for being more than a little confused by all the Gemini AI models Google has pushed out in recent months. For some time now, the models have been split into Flash-Lite, Flash, and Pro, and as you go up that scale, the AI gets slower, more capable at deeper reasoning and complex queries, and more expensive. (Not to mention, these models have different thinking levels too).

With the Pro category, we're still on Gemini 3.1 Pro that launched in February 2026. While a follow-up was mentioned at Google I/O in May, it's yet to be made public. The Flash channel is moving along much more quickly, and it was only a few months ago in December that the first Gemini Flash 3.0 was previewed.

Now we have Gemini 3.8 Flash. As per Google's benchmarks (which you should always take with a pinch of salt), it offers improvements over its predecessor when tackling "long-horizon software engineering" (so full projects rather than small tools), knowledge work (synthesizing and digging into information), complex legal workflows, financial analysis, and agentic activities. Gemini 3.8 Flash is particularly good at complex engineering problems, Google says, and has improved in multi-step reasoning across science, math, humanities, and professional fields. It'll go into more depth to figure answers out, run more checks on their accuracy, and work better at combining different skills in one response.

There are safety measures in place too: The AI has guardrails to block misuse concerning chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cyber offense lines of questioning, and is better than ever at resisting prompt injection attacks (where prompts are engineered to try and get the AI to do something malicious). It all looks impressive on the surface, as do the demos Google showcases here: One of them is a fully working version of Google Maps inside an MS-DOS interface, which will particularly appeal if (like me) you started using computers back in the days of the command prompt.

While I don't have any long-horizon software projects on the go at the moment, I did put the new Gemini 3.8 Flash up against the Gemini 3.6 Flash model that's available to free users in a variety of tasks: designing an interactive Solar System animation, summarizing and simplifying a dense scientific paper, and analyzing the last week of emails in my Gmail account (one of the toughest engineering challenges I know).

To begin with, Gemini 3.8 Flash was noticeably faster: 23 seconds versus 27 seconds for building a space simulation, 15 seconds versus 20 seconds for the science summary, and more or less equal on the emails. Add up those percentages over huge projects and multiple tasks, and you can see that the new model really does get stuff done faster.

For the Solar System test, the simulations were pretty similar—perhaps a sign of how fast they've progressed that a task like this is straightforward for them now. Gemini 3.8 Flash did do a slightly better job at the quality of the renderings though, as the planets look noticeably more "real." When it came to the science summary, again both AI models tackled a tricky problem well. If anything, Gemini 3.6 Flash presented a more understandable summary—perhaps as it's a simpler model—but I found the visualizations and diagrams presented by Gemini 3.8 Flash more helpful (remember the images are created by Nano Banana 2 in both cases, but the info is provided by the underlying model).

On the email challenge, there wasn't much to choose between them: Both accurately summarized what was in my inbox and picked out the same items that needed attention (emails that weren't that important as it happens, but that's a whole other story). This is still a job I prefer to do myself, but these AI models are getting more reliable.

The speed and sophistication gains that Google has talked about are clearly there, even in small-scale tests like this—and it's notable that creating mini web apps and digging through complex physics papers are now straightforward for Flash models as well as the Pro equivalents, which is maybe something to think about if you're considering signing up for a Google AI plan. (Of course, if you want to upgrade to Gemini 3.8 Flash, you'll need to pay.)

Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela Scanlon

John Lewis is launching an online chatshow and social media studio to help make itself and its products more visible to chatbots and more prominent in AI search results.

The department store chain’s Gift List “vodcast” hosted by the TV presenter Angela Scanlon will air on YouTube with clips disseminated via other social media channels and comes after the success of its sister chain Waitrose’s Dish podcast.

The premise is guests discussing good and bad presents they have given and received, with the broadcaster Louis Theroux appearing on the first show. There will be six episodes running up to Christmas, with more planned if the series takes off.

Shoppers are increasingly influenced by the likes of ChatGPT and Gemini to find and recommend products and also by information on social media such as Instagram and TikTok. The AI large language models tend to prioritise third-party advice and live content when formulating their responses, which is forcing retailers to change their marketing plans.

The department store’s outgoing boss, Peter Ruis, said that a year ago just 0.3% of its customers were searching for products via AI large language models such as ChatGPT, but that had already risen to 2.5%, and usage was growing exponentially with all ages using the technology.

Being able to rapidly respond to trends and interests with clips of influencers or experts filmed for social media – such as the opening of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which is expected to spur an interest in cross stitching, or the launch of the Harry Potter TV series before Christmas – has become just as important as the group’s festive TV ad or its ‘never knowingly undersold’ price pledge.

Ruis, who departs John Lewis this weekend after almost three years as managing director, said John Lewis had to move with the times as it faced an economy which was “a bit swirly”.

He said the chancellor’s budget announcements next month would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates.

Ruis said strong trading this week and a string of recent innovations, including modernised cafes and sports departments as well as the social media push and a recent “toy boom”, made him optimistic about the run-up to Christmas.

Details of John Lewis’s half-year figures will be released next week. Ruis said it had been a “summer of winners and losers” but indicated there was now “decent momentum” as shoppers still had money to spend.

The chain rang up record sales of garden furniture, fans and air conditioning over the summer but Ruis said it was not yet clear if the “Burnham bounce” over the summer would last. “People are not going to splurge when you have got inflation swirling,” he said.

“It’s not an easy economy. It’s not easy for customers and inflation is kicking in and the fuel pump is costing people a lot of money.”

Ruis last month announced his abrupt departure, saying he was going to “pursue new projects”. He gave no further clue on his future plans on Thursday but said there was “no misalignment” on strategy with John Lewis’s relatively new chair, Jason Tarry.

“We are getting things done at pace,” Ruis said, adding there was “never a good time” to leave but it was “far better to leave a winning team at the top of its game and all that excitement with events next year to unveil, rather than finishing bottom of the league and running out of the door”.

Ruis insisted his departure did not indicate that he had lost hope in the future of John Lewis, saying it was not a traditional department store reliant on fashion and beauty like Harvey Nichols, which was bought out of administration by Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group last month.

He said John Lewis sold a third of all UK prams and pushchairs, garden furniture and the latest technology and “this is not stuff Harvey Nichols can sell”.

Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips

Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.

Shares ⁠in Nvidia were ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.

The New York-based startup Hugging Face, which is backed by Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.

The chipmaker is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.

Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate, test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.

Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying the technology. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.

There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future.

“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention programme of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.

For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply constrained processors.

Hugging Face has also been ​in the news recently after a hack by rogue AI agents that ​escaped OpenAI’s testing ‌environment. Beyond hosting AI ​models, it offers datasets, ​software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.

title: The Fight for Serious AI Regulation Just Won a Big Victory in Massachusetts
description: John...
fullText:
After his primary win, Ed Markey says he’s ready to take on “the criminal enterprises” of Big Tech.

Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey won a major primary election victory on Tuesday, claiming another win for the left in this summer’s struggle for the soul of the Democratic Party. “Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey declared to a cheering crowd in which his young supporters celebrated a 65–35 triumph over his primary rival, US Representative Seth Moulton.

It was also, the senator explained, a victory in the fight against what he described as “the criminal enterprises of Big Oil and Big Tech.” A longtime foe of corporate greed and monopoly, Markey made stymieing the plans of AI oligarchs a crucial part of his campaign. With progressive-populist enthusiasm, he promised to “tax the rich, block the bombs, and stop data centers from polluting our communities.”

This is not a new fight for Markey. As the senator noted earlier this year, he’s been “working for more than a decade to propose commonsense policies to take back unchecked power from Big Tech and put it into the hands of the American people.”

But what made Markey’s victory notable was that, in the last days of the primary campaign, he faced and overcame a cynical attack from Moulton, who attempted to dumb down the AI debate in a way that he thought would turn voters against the incumbent.

Moulton’s primary challenge to Markey was always tough to fathom. A middle-aged congressman with limitless ambition but finite political skills—as evidenced by his failed bid for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination—Moulton tried to make the fight a generational struggle between a 47-year-old rival and an 80-year-old incumbent. The message never got traction because Markey campaigned relentlessly as an energetic progressive legislator with a record of standing on the right side of history.

Yet Moulton’s desperation to make the race a referendum on youth-versus-age made the last days before Tuesday’s primary contest an instructive measure of the emerging discourse over AI regulation.

When the two candidates clashed in a pre-primary debate last month, Markey gave an uninspired answer to a silly question about whether he uses AI tools on his electronic devices. He basically said he used the apps that were on his iPhone and iPad and left it at that.

Moulton, who talked during the campaign about “winning the AI race while making sure our kids, our economy, and our communities are protected,” seized on what he thought was an opening to catch up with an incumbent who was opening a wide lead in the polls. “Not understanding the basics of AI—the most important technology of our lifetime—should be disqualifying for a U.S. Senator,” he announced on social media. “This is why we need a new generation of leadership. The future is now.”

Then he pinned the message to the top of his X feed. Then he made a campaign ad. Then the challenger said, “Americans are genuinely concerned about AI. Octogenarians in the Senate are not helping.”

The campaigns also traded charges about Moulton’s investment in defense contractors, including “an AI firm that partners with the U.S. Army,” and how Markey had received the support of a nonprofit backed by Anthropic, a firm that has supported AI regulation

Amid all this bluster, Markey kept his cool, while Moulton revealed his naïveté regarding the debate over AI.

That debate is about a lot more than ruminations on the relative merits of ChatGPT and Claude. It is a fight over who will set the rules for our future.

The mounting pressure to meet the demands of the AI billionaires—to whom Donald Trump pays so much deference—raises fundamental questions about corporate power, privacy, the future of work, and a host of other issues. These are issues that Markey—long a leading Senate advocate for worker rights and consumer protection—has been focused on for years. And they are issues on which he has displayed far more insight and agility than most members of Congress.

Obituary

 /

 Nick Murray

Markey’s detailed “AI Accountability Agenda: Taking Power Back From Big Tech” program pulls together groundbreaking legislative proposals to regulate data centers and to address the broader impacts of AI—including the No Robot Bosses Act, which “would prohibit an employer from primarily relying on automated systems for work-related decisions such as hiring, firing, or promotion. The legislation would also require employers to disclose to their employees their use of an automated decision system; conduct detailed evaluations of an automated system’s impact on workers before using the system; and provide an employee with the option to appeal to a human any decision involving an automated system.”

The senator has also proposed and supported legislation to create a human override option for AI decisions that might limit access to healthcare, infringe on privacy rights, or endanger children, and to prevent AI-powered algorithms from amplifying the biases and discrimination that is already embedded in society.

Markey’s even got a plan to prevent the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of AI oligarchs. His Equal Tax Act “would tax investment income at the same rate as ordinary labor income for individuals making more than $1 million. The bill would limit preferential tax rates for long-term capital gains and dividends, end the stepped-up basis loophole, restrict the use of like-kind exchanges by the ultra-wealthy, and limit the passthrough deduction for high-income individuals. By closing loopholes that reward wealth over work, the Equal Tax Act would ensure that the people who profit most from the AI boom pay their fair share.”

Voters recognize that the fight over AI cannot be reduced to election-eve jibes over which candidate might more ably manipulate apps on a phone. It is an existential struggle over questions of whether those with wealth and power will roll over workers, consumers, and civil rights. “Americans,” Markey has explained, “deserve policymakers who are paying attention to their lives, not Big Tech’s bottom line.” By an overwhelming margin, Massachusetts voters gave Ed Markey a mandate to continue serving as that sort of policymaker.

title: I Let ChatGPT Sign Into My Web Accounts for Me, and It Was More Trouble Than It’s Worth
description: This isn't quite the future of web browsing and account access yet.
fullText:
AI agents are becoming more capable over time, and the latest ability rolled out to ChatGPT Work (that's the agentic bit of ChatGPT) is being able to sign into websites—and in theory, taking even more of your workload off you. The official examples of how you might want to use this include setting up utilities for a new apartment, organizing an appointment with a doctor, and canceling tickets for a rescheduled trip. "If it's something you’d normally have to open a browser and click through yourself, try asking ChatGPT Work to do it," says the sales pitch.

I'm all for saving time on admin, but handing over my login credentials to ChatGPT feels like a bold step. Can I trust ChatGPT to keep my details safe and secure? And what are the chances of it going haywire once it's in my accounts? In the interests of finding out, I let it log into some of my less important accounts to see what it could do.

This feature is rolling out now in the web and mobile apps for those on ChatGPT Plus, Pro, and Business accounts.

According to the ChatGPT release notes for August 25, 2026, "ChatGPT cannot see your username or password, and they are never seen by the model or used in model training. ChatGPT does not store your username or passwords." So how does it work if your usernames or passwords are never stored? The most basic option here is to simply sign in through ChatGPT when prompted by a site or app (and clear any two-factor authentication challenges at the same time), and then have the AI stay logged in for future tasks.

The more advanced version, which is where you save a more significant chunk of time, is to give ChatGPT permission to interface with a third-party password manager. ChatGPT doesn't specify a list of supported password managers, but as far as I can tell, this is just for mobile: Any password manager on your phone can pop up when ChatGPT needs it and supply the relevant credentials.

Underpinning all this is an actual browser, built into ChatGPT, that it can access and operate itself. Your accounts will see it as a new sign in (like they would if you signed in from a new device), and some websites and apps will let you mark ChatGPT as a "trusted" operator that can log in again in the future,

You can control the data held by this browser: From ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Cloud browser. You can delete stored cookies from here, for example, which will effectively kick the AI out of any sites it has access to. As per ChatGPT support: "You stay in control of which websites ChatGPT Work can access, and it will always ask for confirmation before consequential actions, such as completing a reservation or payment." Exactly how it can tell when it's about to do something consequential, however, isn't clear.

If you want to make use of this inside ChatGPT on the web, click Work at the top of the screen to switch to agent mode, then tell the AI what you want to do: Something like "sign into my eBay account and tell me how my auctions are doing" or "sign into my accounting app and submit these invoices."

I gave the eBay one a go first—the process proved to be incredibly slow for whatever reason, and I could've signed in multiple times in the normal way by the time ChatGPT got around to gaining access. There are also problems where the ChatGPT conversation tends to obfuscate what's going on: It asked for a verification code, and I didn't know where to check for it.

You can, at any point, switch to the ChatGPT browser itself, which I eventually did to get through the verification code stage (it was sent over text). The AI was then able to correctly tell me what the current auction prices were on the items I was bidding on, after initially stumbling through several wrong pages—there's a thumbnail of the live browser in the corner of the screen, so you can see what's happening.

Next up, I tasked ChatGPT with getting into my Airbnb account and finding some great spots close to Santa Cruz, Calif., within a certain price range. Again, I had to switch to the actual browser view to sign in (I was told the Airbnb site wasn't cooperating), but once I had given the AI access, it worked smoothly enough, looking up properties and giving me a rundown of prices.

At the moment, the sign-in flows are just too finicky. Sites seem suspicious of the AI browser, everything is really slow, and you run into complications with verification codes, passkeys, and the like. You'll often have to manually sign in as you would anyway in order to get ChatGPT up and running on a site.

Once that's done, though, everything works reasonably impressively, as long as you're giving commands that are fairly easy to interpret and carry out. ChatGPT on Airbnb seems competent with dates and locations, but I'm not sure it could filter through places based on the view or the general vibe of the decor.

Perhaps most importantly, I still don't trust the AI to do these jobs better than I can, even if it can (eventually) do it more quickly. I want to see for myself what an Airbnb looks like, or who's bidding on an eBay auction, or what the available time slots are for an appointment to get my car serviced—if I left it to ChatGPT, I'd be too worried about it missing something (I have the same reservations about letting friends and family do things for me as well, but that's another issue).

In my testing, ChatGPT didn't fail in any of the tasks I gave it once it had gained access to these sites, or give me any inaccurate answers, but that would always be at the back of my mind if I switched over to this completely. For now, I'm going to stick to these online admin tasks myself.

title: WeatherNext 3: Our most advanced global weather AI model
description: WeatherNext 3, our most advanced global weather AI model, is now in Search, Gemini, Maps, Google Maps Platform, and Cloud.
fullText:
Our flagship AI weather forecasting model now includes real-time satellite data, hourly refreshes, higher resolution, precise precipitation forecasting, and clean energy variables. It’s now integrated across Search, Gemini, Maps, Google Maps Platform, and Cloud.

Every day, the weather influences billions of decisions. Some are as simple as grabbing an umbrella before heading out the door, but others are far more consequential. Wind, rain, and extreme weather events, like heatwaves and droughts, have cascading impacts across agriculture, global supply chains, clean energy production, and national economies.

In recent years, AI has revolutionized weather forecasting, using historical records to make faster and more accurate predictions than traditional methods. Yet predicting highly local and rapidly changing weather has remained a challenge. Previous models often lacked sufficient spatial resolution, and struggled to incorporate real-time weather data from sources like satellites.

Today, Google DeepMind and Google Research are introducing WeatherNext 3, the most advanced and accurate global weather model to date, according to independent live evaluations by Brightband. Our model learns directly from real-time observations, enabling it to provide timely and more localized predictions for the weather events that impact people the most. By using raw satellite data to produce a forecast every hour in high resolution, our model makes reliable forecasts accessible across Google products worldwide.

A forecast's utility often comes down to detail and how finely it resolves both time and space. WeatherNext 3 generates hourly forecasts at multiple spatial resolutions, maintaining physical consistency from broad global wind patterns all the way down to local topography.

With WeatherNext 3, we can visualize key surface variables — like temperature and moisture — at a 5-kilometer resolution, other surface variables at 10 kilometers, and atmospheric variables, like wind speed, at 25 kilometers. Overall, this provides a global weather picture roughly five times sharper than our previous model, WeatherNext 2, which produced forecasts on a 25-kilometer grid in 6-hour increments.

Figure 1: The end-to-end WeatherNext 3 system architecture. The model ingests live 1-hour geostationary satellite mosaics alongside traditional historical analysis to feed a single, flexible Functional Generative Network (FGN) mesh transformer. It outputs dense gridded fields, discrete cyclone tracks, and predicts station-level sparse coordinates natively.

Figure 2: Comparison of 2-meter temperature forecasts over the UK. WeatherNext 2 (left) at 25-kilometer (0.25°) resolution vs. WeatherNext 3 (right) at a native 5-kilometer (0.05°) resolution. WeatherNext 3 resolves the intricate local topography, preventing the pixelated, over-smoothed thermal representations seen in older models.

WeatherNext 3's biggest leap forward is what it learns from. Most AI weather models, including WeatherNext 2, are trained on data from numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. Although useful, NWP models are complex, supercomputer-driven physics simulations that carry a six-hour data lag. This lag can lead to biases for fast-changing variables like rain or surface temperature.

This is important because critical weather develops fast. When storms, fronts, or precipitation systems materialize suddenly, our rapid update cycle and higher resolution provides earlier, more detailed insights needed to help drive an effective response.

Some variables, like temperature and humidity, can fluctuate dramatically over just a few kilometers, which is particularly relevant for communities near coastlines, valleys, or mountain ranges. Traditional models struggle here because they train on representations of the atmosphere that lack detail and miss extreme local variations.

To address this, WeatherNext 3 instead trains directly on sparse weather station observation data. This allows us to make global forecasts on a 5-kilometer grid that account for regional details like topography.

This breakthrough is particularly vital for regions across Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific that have historically been underserved by high-resolution forecasting due to the immense supercomputing costs of traditional regional models. It brings localized, high-fidelity forecasting to billions of people and local businesses in these areas.

Beyond improved resolution and forecast frequency, our model introduces predictions specifically engineered for renewable energy production. The model forecasts 100-meter wind speeds (roughly at turbine-height) for precise wind-energy output, alongside high-resolution cloud cover and sun radiation levels to help solar farms estimate how much light they will receive on the ground.

This data is crucial for global clean energy planning, allowing grid operators and renewables developers to accurately predict how much power their clean energy assets will generate and match it with consumer demand.

Global weather models notoriously struggle to accurately predict precipitation. Rain and snow systems are driven by fast-moving cloud processes on tiny scales that are hard to model accurately using traditional physics-based simulations. Consequently, AI forecasts often produce blurry estimates or miss the boundaries of severe storms entirely.

To solve this, we train our model on two exceptionally high-quality sources of precipitation data: NASA’s satellite-based Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) and our own global precipitation reanalysis based on satellite radar.

The result is a significant leap in precipitation forecasting accuracy. In medium-range global forecasts, evaluations against baselines show a Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) improvement of up to 60% against IMERG, 30% for MRMS, and 10% against rain gauge measurements for early lead times.

Figure 3: Medium-range probability of precipitation (PoP > 1mm) forecast comparison. WeatherNext 2 (left) at 25-kilometer resolution shows a highly diffused and pixelated precipitation footprint. WeatherNext 3 (middle) at 11-kilometer resolution closely mirrors the actual satellite ground truth (right), accurately capturing the sharp, convective bands of the weather systems.

Our primary goal is to advance weather intelligence to make it universally useful — whether for an emergency responder tracking sudden wind shifts, an air traffic controller planning flight paths, or a farmer managing crops.

To bring these breakthroughs out of the lab and into the real world, we’re integrating WeatherNext 3 across Google’s core ecosystem and beyond:

The atmosphere will always retain a degree of unpredictability. However, by training on real-world observations and bypassing traditional modeling constraints, WeatherNext 3 brings us closer to a future where forecasts truly match what is happening on the ground.

title: 'Alexa for Shopping' Can Now Help You Spot a Spam Email
description: Amazon's AI might be able to confirm whether or not the company is messaging you.
fullText:
While many internet scams are obvious enough to easily avoid, they are growing more sophisticated. Even seasoned users may find themselves duped by a clever fake email, text, or phone call. Case in point: If you receive a message from "Amazon," you might have trouble quickly identifying whether or not it's legitimate. That could lead you to either fall for a trap, or, if the message is real, miss an important announcement or alert from the company.

There are plenty of tactics and best practices out there for verifying these messages on your own, of course: You can take a look at the email address or phone number that sent it, and do your own research to see whether it's official contact info for the company (depending on the email address, this might be apparent on its own); you can study the body of the message, looking for grammar and spelling mistakes that would give away a hasty phishing scheme; and you can note any financial requests, or time-sensitive demands, which would raise the stakes and increase the chances that someone would treat the message and its contents as legitimate.

But none of these tactics allows you to confirm directly with the company—in this case, Amazon—whether that outreach is real. A new Alexa tool does just that.

On Wednesday, Amazon announced an interesting new initiative aimed at reducing—if not eliminating—the risk of users falling for scams. Starting today, "Alexa for Shopping," Amazon's shopping assistant, will help you verify whether an email, text, or phone call from "Amazon" is actually from the company. The company says you can ask Alexa for Shopping questions like "Did Amazon send me a text about a delivery problem yesterday?" "Is this email about my Prime membership from Amazon real?" or "I got a call about a refund from someone saying they're from Amazon. Was that real?” In addition, you ask Alexa for Shopping 

The AI will use these details to figure out whether the message is something Amazon sent itself. What's unique about this new feature is that the bot can actually check your details against the company's record of "every communication it has sent," including sender information, message content, when messages were sent, and exact formatting. Amazon says it completes this check "within seconds," and you'll receive one of the following answers: confirmed from Amazon, not from Amazon, or unable to verify. Amazon says Alexa for Shopping will only confirm a message is real if it has total certainty.

If the message was from Amazon, the company will confirm that the message type, source, date, and time were all consistent with Amazon's message records. You'll also get tips for keeping your account secure—whether you asked for them or not. If the message is not from Amazon, you might get a result like, “This message does not appear to match any official Amazon communication based on the information provided.” Alexa for Shopping may then follow up with recommendations, like checking your orders in the app, contacting Amazon directly, and warnings against clicking links or replying to the message. If it can't confirm the message, Amazon may encourage you to try another verification method.

This isn't the first verification method Amazon has rolled out. The company says it launched an email address, "[email protected]," earlier this year for users to forward messages to. There is also an existing Amazon customer service form that walks you through filing a similar request. Alexa for Shopping will likely point you in these directions if it can't verify your message for whatever reason.

While companies continue to shove AI features into all of their products, this one from Amazon seems potentially quite useful. It's such a simple concept that I'm surprised more companies don't already offer a similar service. Why not automatically check user submissions against your message records to help separate real messages from spam? Perhaps Amazon will be a trailblazer here—assuming the feature actually works, and doesn't hallucinate verifications.

fullText:
The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation

The Trump administration is supporting OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train artificial intelligence.

The Times accuses OpenAI and its largest financial backer, Microsoft, of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. Other newspapers have joined in the suit, first filed in 2023.

In a brief filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, the US government weighed in for the first time on lawsuits over the tense battle over AI and copyright. A brief has advisory rather than legal weight but could bolster tech ⁠companies as they fight the claims.

“The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally … As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence’,” the brief said.

For AI chatbots to generate responses, machine learning systems are first fed billions of lines of text. The bots produce their output by statistical analysis of what the next word should be by matching a user’s query to parts of the database.

Spokespeople for the Times and OpenAI did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment on the filing on Wednesday.

“AI dominance is critical to promote national security, prosperity, and economic mobility for all Americans,” US associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr said in a statement posted to X. “This Administration will never let our Nation be at a disadvantage relative to our foreign adversaries based on a plainly incorrect understanding of copyright law.”

The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, separately told G20 officials ‌at a meeting in North Carolina on Wednesday that their countries should embrace fair use and allow AI companies to train their models on creators’ work while finding ​a way to “protect artists”.

All of the pending cases will probably ​revolve around whether AI systems make ​fair use of copyrighted material by ​using it to create new, transformative content. The first two judges to consider the ​question issued diverging rulings ‌last year.

The government ​agreed with ​tech companies in Tuesday’s brief that AI training is “extraordinarily” transformative.

“Beyond the subject matter of this litigation, LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs,” the brief said. “Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”

fullText:
Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings

Uber drivers have launched a landmark legal action against the ride-hailing company claiming they live in “constant fear” of a “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.

Drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings.

The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation.

The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept.

Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty.

“It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept. So the prices go low but you are stuck. It knows you need the job.”

Kola Oba, who calls the algorithm “soulless”, was taking a break in Tottenham, north London, with another driver when they were offered the same job.

The other driver was offered £27 and Oba was offered £23. The pair suspected it was because Oba, 48, had taken several cheap jobs and the AI assumed he would accept a lower price. Uber has previously said such discrepancies were down to other features of its system including GPS, surge pricing, promotions and testing.

“It’s scary – they have all my information and they are using it against my own wellbeing,” Oba said. “It defines how much I earn, how long I have to work, my time with my family, my resting time.”

AI models take an increasing role in assigning work to humans by using their rapidly increasing power to learn about a business’s needs and staff behaviour and then acting as a “synthetic manager”.

The Dutch data protection authority fined ⁠Uber €825m (£708m) last month for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequate notice. Uber said it would appeal. The company is also planning to roll out driverless cars in European cities from London to Zagreb, initially with human supervisions.

The legal case is being led by the Worker Info Exchange, a campaign group whose founder, James Farrar, secured a UK supreme court ruling that Uber drivers should have worker rights.

Relating to about 241,000 drivers across the EU and the UK, the claim alleges that Uber has unlawfully used automated decision-making, including profiling, in dynamically setting pay and allocating work.

The lawsuit, which also claims the company unlawfully used driver data to train its AI models, is seeking damages for affected drivers and an injunction to halt the conduct which it claims breaches GDPR data regulations.

The drivers claim Uber has operated dynamic pay-setting in the UK since 2023, pushing down their annual incomes by about £5,000. The system was introduced in the Netherlands this year.

Uber’s chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, said in 2023: “I think that what we can do better is targeting of different trips to different drivers based on their preferences or based on behavioural patterns that they’re showing us.”

Uber said it did not adjust the price offered for a trip based on an individual driver’s behaviour and that a history of accepting or rejecting trips was not used to personalise pay offers. Instead, it said, dynamic pricing allowed it to increase pay on less attractive trips, boosting a driver’s earning potential.

“While we haven’t seen the claim yet, we categorically reject the allegations,” an Uber spokesperson said. “The Uber app uses real-time information about the trip such as journey, duration and destination to calculate fares.

“Drivers see their earnings and where a trip is going before they decide whether to accept it. The vast majority of total fares continue to go where they belong: into drivers’ pockets, and the percentage that Uber keeps from fares has remained relatively flat.”

A 2025 study by academics at the University of Oxford, which Uber said relied on incomplete and selective data, found there had been substantial cuts in driver earnings after the “dynamic” algorithm was introduced.

Farrar said: “It’s bad enough that Uber’s dynamic pay algorithms have squeezed driver pay for years now but the intrusive and underhanded way in which Uber uses its technology to monitor and influence drivers’ behaviour is an affront to their dignity as workers and as human beings.”

Anton Ekker, a Dutch lawyer leading the case, said: “A computer algorithm should not independently make decisions that strip individuals of their livelihood. Like so many other online platforms, it should be held accountable for the large-scale exploitation of vulnerabilities of European citizens.”

fullText:
Teachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’

New York City will ban students’ use of artificial intelligence in public schools through eighth grade, typically age 13 or 14. The prohibition is scheduled to be announced on Wednesday and will go into effect next week.

The change is part of a sweeping overhaul of the use of technology in the US’s largest school district, which enrolls roughly 900,000 students a year. In another policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10. The city’s public school technology policies are closely watched by the rest of the United States.

Teachers and parents have warned against the use of AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children’s mental health and cognitive development, in particular an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “cognitive surrender”, as well as environmental damage.

AI use will only be allowed in high school, which begins in the ninth grade in the US school system. Even then, it will be limited to specific uses, such as learning about the technology itself.

AI “companion chatbots” offering psychological support will also be banned. The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments.

The city’s education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers – sixth through eighth grade – and 30 minutes for elementary school students. But the question remains of how to monitor AI use, since it often takes place outside the school environment.

The new rules follow an initial framework published in March, which used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for. In 2023, the school system forbade students’ use of ChatGPT, though the ban was reversed less than a year later.

The 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration and creative projects, sparked fury among many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient.

In response, the city’s schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had “missed the mark” in their communications, adding his office would carefully review parents’ feedback for incorporation into future rules.

The city had long planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive “guidebook” to take feedback into account, the education department has said.

The department will set up a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts and union representatives. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York’s AI-in-schools policy.

fullText:
Matt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firm

The architect of the UK government’s AI strategy has joined the US startup Anthropic in a senior role a year after stepping down from his Downing Street post.

Matt Clifford, a successful tech investor, was appointed as AI opportunities adviser by Keir Starmer last year but resigned from the unpaid role six months later for personal reasons.

His move to the company behind the Claude chatbot has raised concern, with the head of the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee, Chi Onwurah, saying that his decision to remain as chair of the government-backed Aria funding body represented a “clear conflict of interest”.

Clifford will be Anthropic’s managing director, international affairs, and will lead the company’s engagement with governments outside the US including in the UK, Europe, Asia-Pacific and India.

Anthropic said Clifford would remain as the chair of Aria, the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, which funds “moonshot” science and tech projects. He will also maintain his chair role at Entrepreneurs First, the tech venture capital firm he co-founded.

He was appointed chair of Aria in 2022. Anthropic said Clifford would step back from any matter involving the company at Aria. But Onwurah said the roles clashed and she called on the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, to intervene.

“His intention to remain as chair of Aria, which spends taxpayer money on cutting-edge research, much of it related to or driven by AI, is a clear conflict of interest and I look forward to the AI minister setting out clear boundaries,” Onwurah said.

Anthropic said its commercial relationship with Aria was handled by a separate team to Clifford’s and he did not make procurement or programme-level spending decision at Aria anyway.

“Matt has no involvement in any decision touching Anthropic, and that arrangement has been agreed with Aria and the Department of Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, which is responsible for appointing Aria’s chair,” the company said.

The UK government has been approached for comment.

Several senior politicians have taken roles at Silicon Valley firms in recent years. The former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg took a senior post at Meta in 2018. Last year the former prime minister Rishi Sunak took advisory roles at Microsoft and Anthropic, and the ex-chancellor George Osborne joined OpenAI.

Commenting on his role at Anthropic, Clifford said the most important decisions about AI would be made by companies and governments together. He said: “Countries everywhere want real agency over how this technology is built and used, and my job is to make Anthropic a genuine partner in that – in Europe, Asia and beyond.”

Anthropic is preparing for a stock exchange flotation that could value the business at $2tn (£1.5tn).

Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, said the move showed that “the revolving door is a problem for advisers as much as it is for ministers”.

“Taking extensive knowledge obtained within government, about a policy as sensitive as AI, to a private sector company shortly after leaving government gives that company a huge advantage,” said Brake, a Liberal Democrat MP from 1997 to 2019. “Regardless of any safeguards, this weakens the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.”

Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of the government’s AI policy, said: “We need more independent politics which puts the interests of workers, citizens and society at the forefront of our relationship with the tech sector.”

An Anthropic spokesperson said the UK was “one of dozens” of governments Clifford’s team would engage with. “We hire people with expertise and who understand how government works because our work requires it – in every market, not just the UK,” they said.

Clifford began his tech career in the private sector. Prior to his government work, he was an established figure on the UK tech scene as a co-founder of Entrepreneurs First, which has helped build tech companies with a combined worth of more than $20bn.

Clifford worked with Sunak’s government as his representative to the 2023 AI Safety Summit in the UK, and helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute.

He was appointed as Starmer’s AI adviser after drafting the government’s AI action plan, which supports the creation of AI growth zones to host datacentres and the building of the UK’s own AI models.

title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI
